claim: High-density extracellular electrophysiological recordings were performed across several laminae within primary auditory cortical (AI) columns of rats using broadband dynamic noises.
source: We performed high-density extracellular electrophysiological recordings across several laminae within primary auditory cortical (AI) columns of rats using broadband dynamic noises (Atencio and Schreiner, 2010a; 2010b).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: The cortical column is a fundamental organizing substrate within the AC, and relates neurons with similar preferred frequencies.
source: The cortical column is a fundamental organizing substrate within the AC, and relates neurons with similar preferred frequencies (Wallace and Palmer, 2008 (gerbil); Atencio and Schreiner, 2010a, 2010b (cat); Guo et al., 2012 (mouse); but see Winkowski and Kanold, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The ketamine-anesthetized preparation was chosen to enhance the stability of the recordings over time and to reduce the influence of state changes on neural networks.
source: We chose the ketamine-anesthetized preparation to enhance the stability of the recordings over time and to reduce the influence of state changes on neural networks; the awake (Fritz et al., 2005; McGinley et al., 2015; Okun et al., 2010; Poulet and Petersen, 2008) or urethane-anesthetized (Clement et al., 2008; Marguet and Harris, 2011; Pagliardini et al., 2013) rat cortex would undergo state changes more frequently, potentially affecting the composition of cNEs.
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning for the choice of anesthesia with supporting citations.

claim: Dimensionality reduction techniques were applied to recorded populations to identify coordinated neuronal ensembles (cNEs), which consisted of neurons that exhibited sharply synchronous activity.
source: We applied dimensionality reduction techniques to recorded populations and identified cNEs, which consisted of neurons that exhibited sharply synchronous activity (Lopes-dos-Santos et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical method used with a citation.

claim: cNEs have higher coincident firing than can be explained from receptive field similarity or second-order (pairwise) correlations.
source: Our results show that cNEs can be accurately and reliably detected, have higher coincident firing than can be explained from receptive field similarity or second-order (pairwise) correlations, and have active events that occur more frequently than expected from population recordings.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a result of the study.

claim: cNEs identified from spontaneous and evoked epochs were highly similar, implying that cNEs represent functional networks that are not dependent on stimulus presentation.
source: cNEs identified from spontaneous and evoked epochs were highly similar, implying that cNEs represent functional networks that are not dependent on stimulus presentation.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a finding from the study.

claim: cNEs encode auditory information more reliably than single neurons or random groups of neurons with similar receptive fields.
source: Our results also show that cNEs encode auditory information more reliably than single neurons or random groups of neurons with similar receptive fields and support the notion that cNEs represent unique and functionally significant units of processing in AI.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a result of the study.

claim: Single-unit activity in isolation is often insufficient to account for observed sensory or motor behaviors.
source: Single-unit activity in isolation, however, is often insufficient to account for observed sensory or motor behaviors (Bizley et al., 2010; Britten et al., 1996; Engineer et al., 2008; Georgopoulos et al., 1986; Herzfeld et al., 2015; Paninski et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Technological advances in large-scale recordings have allowed the monitoring of the simultaneous activity of large populations of neurons.
source: Technological advances in large-scale recordings, including calcium imaging and high-density multi-channel electrodes, have allowed the monitoring of the simultaneous activity of large populations of neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Coordinated neuronal activities are postulated to be local network events that reflect improved associations with decision-making, predictions of perceptual events, memory formation, and behavioral performance over isolated single-unit activity.
source: These concerted neuronal activities are postulated to be local network events that reflect improved associations with decision-making, predictions of perceptual events, memory formation, and behavioral performance over isolated single-unit activity (Bathellier et al., 2012; Bell et al., 2016; Gulati et al., 2014; Ince et al., 2013; Kiani et al., 2014; Laubach et al., 2000; Peyrache et al., 2009; Reimann et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Coordinated ensembles have been postulated to be elementary units of information processing in the brain.
source: Coordinated ensembles have also been postulated to be elementary units of information processing in the brain (for review see Buzsáki, 2010; Harris and Mrsic-Flogel, 2013; Yuste, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: STRFs of neurons from the same columnar penetration showed general similarities in characteristic frequency and frequency tuning, and displayed minor variations in spectral and temporal details.
source: STRFs of neurons from the same columnar penetration showed general similarities in characteristic frequency and frequency tuning, and displayed minor variations in spectral and temporal details (see example in Figure 1C), similar to cat cortical columnar recordings (Atencio and Schreiner, 2010a).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in the manuscript and compared to previous research.

claim: Pairs of neurons in the same column with similar STRFs could exhibit widely differing pairwise correlation (PWC) functions.
source: Pairs of neurons in the same column with similar STRFs could nonetheless exhibit widely differing pairwise correlation (PWC) functions (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: PWC sharpness and delay covaried with correlation coefficients, accounting for ~50% of the variance.
source: Across all penetrations, PWCs were fairly heterogeneous but sharpness and delay covaried with correlation coefficients, accounting for ~50% of the variance (Figure 2B–2D).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figures 2B-2D.

claim: The degree of synchrony between pairs of neurons often weakens as the distance between neurons within a column increases.
source: The degree of synchrony between pairs of neurons often weakens as the distance between neurons within a column increases (Atencio and Schreiner, 2013; Gururangan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The correlation between synchrony aspects and pairwise distance only explained ~10–30% of the total variance.
source: We observed similar trends in columnar recordings, although the correlation between these synchrony aspects and pairwise distance only explained ~10–30% of the total variance (R2 values, Figure 2E–2G).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figures 2E-2G.

claim: The cNE detection algorithm combined two dimensionality reduction techniques - principal component analysis (PCA) and independent component analysis (ICA).
source: To identify synchronously firing groups of neurons, or coordinated neuronal ensembles (cNEs), we combined two dimensionality reduction techniques - principal component analysis (PCA) and independent component analysis (ICA), following the approach by Lopes-dos-Santos et al., 2013.
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical method used with a citation.

claim: Application of PCA to the simultaneously recorded spike trains determines the number of cNEs above a significance criterion.
source: Application of PCA to the simultaneously recorded spike trains determines the number of cNEs above a significance criterion (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical method used.

claim: ICA is applied to the significant eigenvectors or principal components (PCs) to extract the linear combination of the individual neurons' activity associated with each cNE.
source: ICA is then applied to the significant eigenvectors or principal components (PCs) to extract the linear combination of the individual neurons' activity associated with each cNE (Lopes-dos-Santos et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical method used with a citation.

claim: The cNE detection algorithm typically identified several independent cNEs, each capturing moments of joint activity between several of its members.
source: The cNE detection algorithm typically identified several independent cNEs, each capturing moments of joint activity between several of its members.
evidence: The manuscript describes the results of the analytical method.

claim: Approximately 96% of independent components had significant matches between the two interleaved parts of the recording.
source: Approximately 96% of independent components had significant matches (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E), indicating that the two interleaved parts of the recording contained the same independent components and that the cNEs were present throughout the entire recording.
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: Approximately 83% of training cNE activity had significant matches to test cNE activity.
source: Across all penetrations, approximately 83% of training cNE activity had significant matches to test cNE activity.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a result of the study.

claim: cNEs obtained from the first half of the recordings were sufficient to predict the activity of cNEs in the latter half of the recording.
source: Thus, cNEs obtained from the first half of the recordings were sufficient to predict the activity of cNEs in the latter half of the recording.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as an inference from the data.

claim: The time required to traverse a rat AI column of approximately 1500 µm in extent is ~10 ms.
source: Using the propagation speed found in the cat and rat, the time required to traverse a rat AI column of approximately 1500 µm in extent is ~10 ms (Atencio and Schreiner, 2010a; Kubota et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations using data from cited sources.

claim: Receptive field information peaked at bin sizes of approximately 10–15 ms.
source: Receptive field information peaked at bin sizes of approximately 10–15 ms (Figure 5A), implying that the temporal resolution used to obtain cNEs provided the most information about the receptive field preferences of groups of synchronously firing neurons in AI, further supporting our choice.
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: As the spike train temporal bin size increased, the number of recovered cNEs decreased.
source: Indeed, we found that as the spike train temporal bin size increased, the number of recovered cNEs decreased (Figure 5B) and the number of member neurons in each cNE increased (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: The number of member neurons in each cNE increased as the spike train temporal bin size increased.
source: Indeed, we found that as the spike train temporal bin size increased, the number of recovered cNEs decreased (Figure 5B) and the number of member neurons in each cNE increased (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: The spike train PWCs were much narrower than the STRF PWCs for neuronal pairs within the same cNE.
source: Comparing STRF PWCs to spike train PWCs (Figure 6A–6F) revealed that the spike train PWCs (Figure 6C, histogram) were much narrower than the STRF PWCs (Figure 6C, solid line) for neuronal pairs within the same cNE.
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figures 6A-6F.

claim: For non-cNE pairs, the spike train PWCs were often as wide as the STRF PWCs.
source: In contrast, for non-cNE pairs, the spike train PWCs were often as wide as the STRF PWCs (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 6F.

claim: The PWCs were significantly narrower for cNE pairs than for non-cNE pairs.
source: The PWCs were significantly narrower for cNE pairs than for non-cNE pairs (p < 0.001, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 6J; see Figure 6—figure supplement 1 for each of the other penetrations).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The median PWC sharpness for member neurons was ~2 ms.
source: The median PWC sharpness for member neurons was ~2 ms, reflecting the central peak of a highly synchronized portion of spikes (Figure 6C and G).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figures 6C and 6G.

claim: Across 16 penetrations, a total of 104 cNEs were identified.
source: Across 16 penetrations, we identified a total of 104 cNEs (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), obtained in response to either DMR or RN broadband stimuli.
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average number of cNEs per penetration was 6.5 ± 2.0.
source: The average number of cNEs per penetration was 6.5 ± 2.0, but the higher the number of neurons isolated in a penetration, the higher the number of identified cNEs (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: For each penetration, the number of cNEs was ~15% of the recorded number of neurons.
source: For each penetration, the number of cNEs was ~15% of the recorded number of neurons.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a result of the study.

claim: The mean number of neurons in cNEs was 7.4 ± 2.5 neurons.
source: The mean number of neurons in cNEs was 7.4 ± 2.5 neurons.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a result of the study.

claim: Mean cNE size was ~17% of the total number of recorded neurons in the column.
source: This again depended on the number of isolated neurons (Figure 7B), with mean cNE size ~17% of the total number of recorded neurons in the column.
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: 9 cNEs (8.3%) contained at least one neuron with a negative weight.
source: However, 9 cNEs (8.3%) also contained at least one neuron with a negative weight, indicating that such neurons had to be inactive at the time of a cNE event.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a result of the study.

claim: A majority (~68%) of neurons belonged to a single cNE.
source: Of the 655 neurons that were isolated, a majority (~68%) belonged to a single cNE, ~9% did not belong to any cNE, and ~23% belonged to multiple cNEs (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 7C.

claim: ~9% of neurons did not belong to any cNE.
source: Of the 655 neurons that were isolated, a majority (~68%) belonged to a single cNE, ~9% did not belong to any cNE, and ~23% belonged to multiple cNEs (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 7C.

claim: ~23% of neurons belonged to multiple cNEs.
source: Of the 655 neurons that were isolated, a majority (~68%) belonged to a single cNE, ~9% did not belong to any cNE, and ~23% belonged to multiple cNEs (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 7C.

claim: A majority of pairs of neurons within the same cNE (~82%) tended to be recorded from channels separated by <200 µm.
source: A majority of pairs of neurons within the same cNE (~82%) tended to be recorded from channels separated by <200 µm (Figure 7D), indicating that cNEs are mostly spatially confined.
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 7D.

claim: Most isolated cNEs (~70%) spanned a depth range of 200 µm or less of the cortical column.
source: Most isolated cNEs (~70%) spanned a depth range of 200 µm or less of the cortical column, again indicating that cNE activity reflects local circuit properties, even though there were a few cNEs that spanned most of the measured cortical column (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 7F.

claim: Approximately 72% of spontaneous and evoked cNEs had significant matches.
source: Across all eight recordings comprising contiguous epochs of spontaneous and evoked activity we found significant matches for ~72% of spontaneous and evoked cNEs (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figures 8D and 8E.

claim: cNEs largely reflect functional connectivity and are not simply a reflection of stimulus-induced synchrony of neurons with overlapping receptive fields.
source: This implies that cNEs largely reflect functional connectivity and are not simply a reflection of stimulus-induced synchrony of neurons with overlapping receptive fields.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as an inference from the data.

claim: The MI conveyed by cNE events was ~10% higher than the MI of each member neuron.
source: The cNE event rasters showed less trial-to-trial variability than individual neuron rasters (Figure 9A and B), and the MI conveyed by cNE events was, accordingly, ~10% higher than the MI of each member neuron (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of data presented in Figures 9A-9C.

claim: The ratio of the MIs (cNE/neuron) was significantly larger than 1.
source: Correspondingly, the ratio of the MIs (cNE/neuron) was significantly larger than 1 (median ± median absolute deviation = 1.11 ± 0.13; p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 9D).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 9D.

claim: The MI of spikes from cNE members was significantly higher than the MI of spikes from random groups of neurons.
source: We found that the MI of spikes from cNE members was significantly higher than the MI of spikes from random groups of neurons (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 9—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 9—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Pairs of neurons that were members of the same cNE had significantly higher noise correlations than pairs of neurons not within the same cNE.
source: Over the 16 columnar recordings, pairs of neurons that were members of the same cNE had significantly higher noise correlations than pairs of neurons not within the same cNE (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: cNE STRFs had stronger excitatory and inhibitory subfields than their member neurons.
source: cNE STRFs had stronger excitatory and inhibitory subfields than their member neurons (Figure 10A).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 10A.

claim: Compared to neuronal STRFs, cNE STRFs had higher peak-trough differences (PTD).
source: Compared to neuronal STRFs, cNE STRFs had higher peak-trough differences (PTD; p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 10B) and MI (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 10C).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 10B.

claim: Compared to neuronal STRFs, cNE STRFs had higher MI.
source: Compared to neuronal STRFs, cNE STRFs had higher peak-trough differences (PTD; p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 10B) and MI (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 10C).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 10C.

claim: The STRF PTD for cNE members was significantly higher than that of the STRF PTD for random groups of neurons.
source: Across the entire population, the STRF PTD for cNE members was significantly higher than that of the STRF PTD for random groups of neurons (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 10—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 10—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The STRF MI of cNE member neurons was significantly higher than that of random groups of neurons.
source: The STRF MI of cNE member neurons was also significantly higher than that of random groups of neurons (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 10—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 10—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The 'surrogate' spike train matrices had fewer cNEs than the 'real' spike train matrices.
source: We found, however, that the 'surrogate' spike train matrices had fewer cNEs (Figure 11A) and that the detected cNEs had fewer member neurons (Figure 11B).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figures 11A and 11B.

claim: The detected cNEs in 'surrogate' spike train matrices had fewer member neurons than those in 'real' spike train matrices.
source: We found, however, that the 'surrogate' spike train matrices had fewer cNEs (Figure 11A) and that the detected cNEs had fewer member neurons (Figure 11B).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figures 11A and 11B.

claim: The number of cNEs identified in the 'real' data is significantly higher than that of the 'shuffled' and 'PR' models, but is significantly lower than that of the 'DG' model.
source: Surrogate spike trains from the 'shuffled' and 'PR' models had significantly fewer cNEs (Figure 11C) than the real data. On the other hand, the 'DG' model overestimates the number of detected cNEs (Figure 11C).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 11C.

claim: All three models ('shuffled', 'PR', and 'DG') resulted in cNEs that were smaller in size than the real data.
source: Despite that, all three models, including the 'DG' model, resulted in cNEs that were smaller in size (i.e., fewer member neurons, Figure 11D) than the real data (n = 16 penetrations; mean values for each penetration were calculated over 200 iterations for each model).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 11D.

claim: The normalized CR for the repeated stimulus data ('repeat'), 'shuffled', 'PR' and 'DG' models were significantly less than one for all groups.
source: The normalized CR for the repeated stimulus data ('repeat'), 'shuffled', 'PR' and 'DG' models were significantly less than one for all groups (Figure 11E and F).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figures 11E and 11F.

claim: For groups containing more than three members, the CR values for most control models were always near or at 0.
source: For groups containing more than three members, the CR values for most control models were always near or at 0 (not shown).
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a result of the study.

claim: Each identified cNE comprised a subset of ~15–20% of the simultaneously recorded neurons.
source: Each identified cNE comprised a subset of ~15–20% of the simultaneously recorded neurons.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a result of the study.

claim: The spatial distribution of neurons within most cNEs was contained within <250 μm of columnar depth, approximately corresponding to the width of granular and supragranular layers.
source: The spatial distribution of neurons within most cNEs was contained within <250 μm of columnar depth, approximately corresponding to the width of granular and supragranular layers.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a result of the study.

claim: Several cNEs encompassed neurons distributed across multiple layers.
source: However, several cNEs encompassed neurons distributed across multiple layers.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a result of the study.

claim: The group spiking events associated with each cNE were more reliable and conveyed more information about the stimulus than spikes of individual neurons or random groups of neurons.
source: The group spiking events associated with each cNE were more reliable and conveyed more information about the stimulus than spikes of individual neurons or random groups of neurons (matched to cNE size).
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a result of the study.

claim: The frequency of occurrence of cNE events was higher than predicted from basic receptive field similarities within the column.
source: We verified that identified cNEs were not chance constructs as a result of stimulus-driven synchronization alone by showing that the frequency of occurrence of cNE events was higher than predicted from basic receptive field similarities within the column.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a result of the study.

claim: A high percentage of cNEs had matching neuronal composition during evoked and spontaneous activations.
source: Since a high percentage of cNEs had matching neuronal composition during evoked and spontaneous activations, these findings support the concept that cNEs are stable local units of information processing in the cortical column.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a result of the study.

claim: Auditory cortical neurons are responsive to envelope modulations occurring over tens of milliseconds.
source: Since auditory cortical neurons are responsive to envelope modulations occurring over tens of milliseconds.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The optimal window for dendritic integration is approximately 10-15 ms.
source: This temporal resolution also agrees with other studies on the optimal window for dendritic integration (Branco and Häusser, 2011; Polsky et al., 2004; Williams and Stuart, 2002) and spike-timing dependent plasticity (Bi and Poo, 1998; Celikel et al., 2004; Markram et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The optimal window for spike-timing dependent plasticity is approximately 10-15 ms.
source: This temporal resolution also agrees with other studies on the optimal window for dendritic integration (Branco and Häusser, 2011; Polsky et al., 2004; Williams and Stuart, 2002) and spike-timing dependent plasticity (Bi and Poo, 1998; Celikel et al., 2004; Markram et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: cNEs may be conveyors of specific environmental information that is either externally triggered or internally engaged.
source: Our data suggest that cNEs may be conveyors of specific environmental information that is either externally triggered or internally engaged.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as an interpretation of the data.

claim: cNEs are tightly locked to stimulus features that trigger ensemble responses.
source: Since information necessarily includes timing information, this implies that cNEs are tightly locked to stimulus features that trigger ensemble responses.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as an inference from the data.

claim: cNEs integrate complementary spiking information from member neurons during stimulus presentations to increase the number of events that respond to stimulus segments with high projection values and to better encode the stimulus.
source: Given the probabilistic nature of neuronal spiking even for the highest projection values, it suggests that cNEs integrate complementary spiking information from member neurons during stimulus presentations to increase the number of events that respond to stimulus segments with high projection values and to better encode the stimulus.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Spikes that occur during stimulus segments with low projection values do not tend to be synchronous with spikes from other neurons and are less likely to be associated with cNE events.
source: On the other hand, spikes that occur during stimulus segments with low projection values do not tend to be synchronous with spikes from other neurons and are less likely to be associated with cNE events (see Figures 4D, E, 9A and B).
evidence: The manuscript presents this as an interpretation of the data with reference to figures.

claim: If one purpose of synchronous firing by groups of neurons is to produce a more efficacious downstream effect than can be accomplished by a single neuron, then cNEs may be the functional units that serve to maintain and/or enhance the fidelity of the encoding of relevant sound features.
source: If one purpose of synchronous firing by groups of neurons is to produce a more efficacious downstream effect than can be accomplished by a single neuron (Buzsáki, 2010), then cNEs may be the functional units that serve to maintain and/or enhance the fidelity of the encoding of relevant sound features.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: cNEs are likely part of larger networks that can span more than a column and extend over several hierarchical levels.
source: They are likely part of larger networks that can span more than a column and extend over several hierarchical levels.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a speculative interpretation.

claim: The relative constancy of cNEs can provide stable spatio-temporal firing patterns with transient multi-neuronal synchrony that may signal salient spectro-temporal events or contribute to the learning and extraction of stimulus categorization.
source: The relative constancy of cNEs can provide stable spatio-temporal firing patterns with transient multi-neuronal synchrony that may, among other functions, signal salient spectro-temporal events (Hopfield and Brody, 2001) or contribute to the learning and extraction of stimulus categorization (Higgins et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a speculative interpretation with citations.

claim: All experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the University of California, San Francisco.
source: All experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the University of California, San Francisco.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a fact about the experimental procedures.

claim: Female Sprague-Dawley rats (200–300 g, 2–3 months old; RRID:MGI:5651135) were anesthetized with a mixture of ketamine and xylazine.
source: Female Sprague-Dawley rats (200–300 g, 2–3 months old; RRID:MGI:5651135) were anesthetized with a mixture of ketamine and xylazine, supplemented with dexamethasone, atropine and meloxicam.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Recordings for all data except Figure 8 were made using a 32-channel probe.
source: Recordings for all data except Figure 8 were made using a 32-channel probe (a1 × 32-poly3, NeuroNexus, Figure 1A), and recording data for Figure 8 was made using a 64-channel probe (H3, Cambridge NeuroTech), inserted perpendicular to the cortical surface to a depth of approximately 800 or 1400 µm respectively using a microdrive (David Kopf Instruments).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental methodology.

claim: The 32-channel traces were spike-sorted offline with a Bayesian spike-sorting algorithm.
source: The 32-channel traces were spike-sorted offline with a Bayesian spike-sorting algorithm that included a spike-waveform decomposition procedure to extract single-unit spike timing (Lewicki, 1994).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical methodology with a citation.

claim: The 64-channel traces were spike-sorted offline using MountainSort, a fully automated spike sorter.
source: The 64-channel traces were spike-sorted offline using MountainSort, a fully automated spike sorter (Chung et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical methodology with a citation.

claim: The dynamic moving ripple (DMR) was a temporally varying broadband sound (500 Hz – 40 kHz) made up of approximately 50 sinusoidal carriers per octave, each with randomized phase.
source: The dynamic moving ripple (DMR) was a temporally varying broadband sound (500 Hz – 40 kHz) made up of approximately 50 sinusoidal carriers per octave, each with randomized phase.
evidence: The manuscript describes the stimulus used in the experiments.

claim: The maximum spectral modulation frequency of the DMR was four cycles/oct, and the maximum temporal modulation frequency was 40 cycles/s.
source: The maximum spectral modulation frequency of the DMR was four cycles/oct, and the maximum temporal modulation frequency was 40 cycles/s.
evidence: The manuscript describes the stimulus used in the experiments.

claim: The ripple noise (RN) stimulus was the sum of 16 independently created DMRs.
source: The ripple noise (RN) stimulus was the sum of 16 independently created DMRs.
evidence: The manuscript describes the stimulus used in the experiments.

claim: Spike-triggered averaging of the DMR and RN was used to recover the spectro-temporal receptive field (STRF) of each neuron.
source: Spike-triggered averaging of the DMR and RN was used to recover the spectro-temporal receptive field (STRF) of each neuron (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical methodology.

claim: Single-unit spike times were binned into 10-ms time bins and normalized via z-scoring.
source: Single-unit spike times were binned into 10-ms time bins and normalized via z-scoring.
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical methodology.

claim: Eigenvalues that exceeded the upper bounds of the Marčenko-Pastur distribution were deemed significant and represented the number of detected cNEs.
source: Eigenvalues that exceeded the upper bounds of the Marčenko-Pastur distribution (Marčenko and Pastur, 1967) were deemed significant and represented the number of detected cNEs.
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical methodology with a citation.

claim: The eigenvectors corresponding to significant eigenvalues were processed using the fast independent component analysis (fastICA) algorithm.
source: The eigenvectors corresponding to significant eigenvalues were then processed using the fast independent component analysis (fastICA) algorithm, which approximates the distance to Gaussianity based on negentropy (Hyvärinen and Oja, 1997).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical methodology with a citation.

claim: The resulting independent components (ICs) represent the contribution of each neuron to each cNE.
source: The resulting independent components (ICs) represent the contribution of each neuron to each cNE.
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical methodology.

claim: The activity of each cNE was calculated by projecting the ICs back onto the z-scored spike matrix.
source: The activity of each cNE was calculated by then projecting the ICs back onto the z-scored spike matrix (Lopes-dos-Santos et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical methodology with a citation.
